body.text: In debates and polemics attacking India, it is frequently asserted that the British made India, ex nihilo, out of whole cloth. Winston Churchill once famously said that “India is a geographical term. It is no more a united nation than the Equator.” In other words, while the idea of a cultural or geographic space known as India is ancient, it exists today as a coherent political unit because the British created it. However, this view is incorrect.

The view that India was a land of many independent kingdoms — rather than a singular Indian state — was not one that was held by Indians themselves in the 18th century, the century during which Great Britain came to govern parts of India. Nor was it the view of the British East India Company (EIC) itself. In 1813, during a petition before the British parliament for the renewal of its charter, the EIC acknowledged that company possessions as dispersed as Lucknow, Surat, Patna, Madras, and Dhaka “were subject to the sovereignty of the great Mogul,” and that the company derived its right to rule territory in India not through the stitching together of independent states but from the authority of the Mughal emperor. It noted that “the Great Mogul granted to the petitioners the country called the Northern Circars … and in the year 1765, the Great Mogul appointed the petitioners, in perpetuity, to the office of dewan [revenue collector] of the provinces of Bengal, Bahar, and Orissa.” The Company was granted these lands and titles after its victory over the forces of the Mughal emperor and the nawabs of Awadh and Bengal at the Battle of Buxar in 1764.
By the 19th century, the EIC ruled India as a sovereign power, but it long continued to acknowledge the fiction of ruling in the Mughal emperor’s name.

According to the East India Company, when it arrived in India in the 17th century, it “found the country [India] divided into many different states, all feudatory to the Mogul, who was considered the sole proprietor of the whole.” The idea of a singular sultanate (saltanat) or empire (mamlakat) of Hindustan, a “territorially defined institutional space” from Delhi (or Agra), dates to the beginning of Muslim rule over the Indian subcontinent during the Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526 CE) and picks up steam during the Mughal Empire (1526-1858 CE), when such rule is associated with the sovereignty of the Timurid (Mughal) dynasty.

It was an enduring idea. Even after the Mughal Empire began to decline in the 18th century, the rulers of India’s now de facto independent Muslim- and Hindu-ruled states continued to exercise power for the most part in its name and did not claim to have founded independent countries. It was, in fact, rare for any ruler to throw off the “pretense of allegiance to the Mughals.”

In Indian and Islamic states, the ultimate marker of sovereignty is coinage: it could only be issued by the permission of, and in the name of, the ruler. In the princely state of Jaipur, all coinage struck until 1857 — the year of the Indian Rebellion that precipitated the end of the empire — was struck in the name of the Mughal emperor. Thereafter, coinage was struck in the name of the British monarch. Likewise, it was only in 1858 that the coinage of Hyderabad state stopped including the emperor’s name.

Additionally, by the late 18th century, essentially independent rulers, such as the maharajas of a number of Maratha states — who also derived their legitimacy from the independent, sovereign Maratha chhatrapati — came to control the Mughal Empire, acquiring high-ranking Mughal titles such as vakil (representative) for legitimacy. In the late 18th century, the Maratha general Mahadaji Shinde became the Vakil-i-Mutlaq, the viceregent of the Mughal Empire, second only to the emperor.

Analogous situations existed in many of the other great empires of Eurasia, many of which had undergone various degrees of decentralization, often spawning de facto independent states that were nonetheless still thought to be parts of a larger polity. Examples include the Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation — which had devolved into a collection of de facto independent states by the time of its dissolution in 1806 — the many eyalets (provinces) of the Ottoman Empire such as Iraq and Tunisia that were ruled by hereditary dynasties, and the han (domains) of Edo Period Japan, which maintained their own local laws and paper currency though they were subject to the rule of the shogun in Edo (Tokyo) and the sovereignty of the emperor in Kyoto.

In all these cases, the tension between regional power centers and centralization either eventually led to the state’s collapse and the emergence of new states or recentralization. Often the reassertion of central authority came about because of the emergence of a new political force, one not weighed down by past baggage. Thus, reformists from the Satsuma and Choshu domains in Japan overthrew the Tokugawa shogunate in 1868 and began a process of aggressive centralization and state consolidation. Likewise, after central authority in Iran nearly collapsed toward the end of the Qajar dynasty, the succeeding Pahlavi dynasty forcefully brought the provinces under tight central control after 1925.

India was no different. By the late 18th century, the central authority of the Mughal Empire had collapsed and several de facto independent states had emerged from its ruins. Assuming the various component states of India did not seek formal, de jure independence, the forces of modernity would have conspired to deliver a similar outcome of consolidation and centralization there, similar to those pursued by Meiji-era Japan and the Tanzimat-era Ottoman Empire after long periods of anarchy and decentralization. Such a policy could only have been undertaken by a group with enough resources and power, legitimacy, or geographic distribution to unite most of the subcontinent: a resconsolidated Mughal state, a newly empowered Maratha empire, or the East India Company.

As it so happened, it was the EIC that reunited India after a century in which it accumulated more and more power and expanded its holdings by annexing local states, most of which did obeisance to the Mughal emperor. It did not create a new country, but took over and appropriated the institutions of a preexisting one while engaging in a policy of consolidation. And finally, in a gradual process, the British crown asserted control over the EIC.

Eventually, in a process lasting from 1813 to 1876, the British government asserted, first, sovereignty over the Company’s holdings — during which the Company officials still also presented themselves as liegemen of the Mughal emperor — before abolishing both the Mughal Empire and the East India Company in 1858. Finally, in 1876, Queen Victoria took the title of Empress of India, being so proclaimed in 1877, filling the empty throne of India and completing the process whereby India transitioned from the rule of the Mughals to the British emperors.
